  Leading question and inferential goals

  What does partisanship itself contribute to the different forms of polarization? "Partisanship" means reporting an attachment, compared with people of the same party who deny one.

  Goals, for each outcome:
  1. A pooled European type contrast
  2. Comparative variation across countries
  3. Dynamic change over time (not for the games)
  4. A decomposition of change and of cross-country differences into the mix of types vs. polarization within types
  5. A profile of type contrasts across outcomes as the party-over-policy diagnostic

  Contributions: comparative research on polarization and behavior, and the US party-over-policy debate. Europe adds leverage the US lacks: attachment and vote come apart, and there are several out-parties at
  different policy distances.

  The four types and what each one adds

  The three voting types are each selected by the vote in a different way. Together they bracket the attachment effect; none of them identifies it alone.

  Table 1: outcomes

  Outcome: 0 Composition
  Data, time: EES, CSES, ESS, eu25; over time
  Unit: respondent
  Polarization quantity: —
  Type estimand: share of each type by country and time
  Multilevel structure: respondents in surveys in countries; trend by country
  Specialities: feeds the decomposition; wording differences between studies are part of the model
  ────────────────────────────────────────
  Outcome: 1 Ideological polarization (LR, EU)
  Data, time: EES, CSES (mostly LR), ESS (EU in some rounds), eu25; over time
  Unit: respondent
  Polarization quantity: extremity (individual); dispersion and bimodality (group)
  Type estimand: Δ extremity within party; group quantities computed on each type's distribution with a common party mix
  Multilevel structure: respondents in party × country × survey; surveys in countries; trend
  Specialities: centre for extremity still open (report alternatives); EU coverage thinner
  ────────────────────────────────────────
  Outcome: 2 Ideological sorting (LR × EU)
  Data, time: where both items exist (EES, ESS rounds, eu25); over time
  Unit: respondent (joint distribution)
  Polarization quantity: strength of the LR–EU association, any shape
  Type estimand: alignment within each type, common party mix
  Multilevel structure: as 1
  Specialities: group-level quantity; nonlinear (inverted U); sign differs by country, so measure within country and pool magnitudes
  ────────────────────────────────────────
  Outcome: 3 Perceived party polarization (LR, EU)
  Data, time: EES, CSES (LR), eu25; over time
  Unit: respondent × placed party
  Polarization quantity: spread of a respondent's placements over a fixed party set; scale-use-corrected stretch as extension
  Type estimand: Δ spread within party; Δ excess over a benchmark (actual positions)
  Multilevel structure: placements in respondents in party × country × survey; time
  Specialities: everyone in a country-survey faces the same real party system
  ────────────────────────────────────────
  Outcome: 4 Perceived party sorting
  Data, time: EES, eu25; over time
  Unit: respondent × placed party
  Polarization quantity: how aligned a respondent's own LR and EU placements are across parties
  Type estimand: Δ perceived alignment; Δ excess over actual alignment
  Multilevel structure: as 3
  Specialities: few parties per respondent, so pool across respondents rather than computing a noisy per-person correlation
  ────────────────────────────────────────
  Outcome: 5 Vertical attitudinal AP (+ EES 2024 horizontal attitudinal)
  Data, time: EES (PTV), CSES (like/dislike), eu25 thermometer; EES 2024 supporter ratings
  Unit: respondent × rated party
  Polarization quantity: in vs. out rating
  Type estimand: $AP_t$ and $\Delta AP$; mismatched respondents have two in-relations (attachment party, vote party); distance gradient
  Multilevel structure: ratings in respondents and target parties; respondents in party × country × survey; time
  Specialities: relation coded per target (attached and voted / attached only / voted only / neither); PTV is not pure affect; EES 2024 fills the horizontal-attitudinal cell
  ────────────────────────────────────────
  Outcome: 6 Horizontal behavioral AP
  Data, time: eu25 games, 2019 only
  Unit: respondent × round
  Polarization quantity: tokens to co vs. out partner
  Type estimand: $AP_t$, $\Delta AP$, split into in-group favoritism (co vs. control) and out-group derogation (control vs. out); control = co-national partner with no party shown
  Multilevel structure: rounds in respondents in party × country
  Specialities: partner party randomized, but stratified by type; beta-binomial ruled out (unimodal, misses the spikes, mean off), so a mean model with cell-specific dispersion plus an ordinal shape check

  Table 2: what the contrast buys, and its limits

  The same for all outcomes:
  - Absorbed: everything shared within party × country: platform, status, the set of out-parties, elite cues, national norms about admitting an attachment.
  - Not absorbed: individual-level confounders of attachment (age and socialization, parental partisanship, interest, ideological intensity).
  - Selection by the vote: the vote can act as a collider, because deniers are selected on their reasons to vote for the party.
  - Measurement: self-labelling and wording effects, plus recall error in the vote.
  - Triangulating across studies addresses wording effects, but not confounding that all studies share.
  - What a causal reading needs: conditional ignorability of attachment given party × country and pre-treatment covariates, no selection on the outcome through the vote, and type meaning the same across
    wordings.

  Outcome family: Composition
  What the contrast buys: description of how the type mix varies across countries and time; the weights for the decomposition
  Boundaries: trends partly reflect switching between studies or wordings
  Causal reading also needs: none (descriptive only)
  Where it likely fails: level comparisons across studies without wording effects
  ────────────────────────────────────────
  Outcome family: Ideology and sorting
  What the contrast buys: rules out "attached partisans are in more extreme parties"; with the common party mix, group quantities aren't driven by party choice
  Boundaries: reverse causation: extreme or coherent people may attach because their views fit a party. Selection on proximity makes deniers look less extreme at centrist parties and more extreme at flank
  parties. Sorting within one party has restricted range
  Causal reading also needs: attachment prior to positions; no proximity selection
  Where it likely fails: the strongest threat: ideology → attachment is at least as plausible as the reverse. Treat as association net of party sorting. The party-position diagnostic tests the selection
  ────────────────────────────────────────
  Outcome family: Perceived polarization and sorting
  What the contrast buys: the real party system is held fixed within country-survey, so perceived differences aren't system differences; a benchmark separates perception from reality
  Boundaries: sophistication raises attachment and may make perceived spread more accurate, not more biased; scale use differs between respondents; the set of placed parties differs by type
  Causal reading also needs: ignorability given sophistication; comparable scale use
  Where it likely fails: the sophistication confound is likely substantial; the benchmark and scale-use correction narrow it, they don't remove it
  ────────────────────────────────────────
  Outcome family: Vertical AP (+ 2024 horizontal attitudinal)
  What the contrast buys: within party, plus within person across targets; target effects absorb how well liked a party is in general; the mismatched A-vs-B comparison is the best-identified quantity; distance

  to the target tests party vs. policy
  Boundaries: the vote as collider: deniers vote for P partly because they dislike the others, which plausibly pulls ΔAP toward zero; out-party sets differ by type; adjusting for distance gives a controlled
  direct effect (distance is partly a consequence of attachment); PTV mixes liking with viability
  Causal reading also needs: no selection on the outcome through the vote; no "dislike of others → attachment" path (negative partisanship)
  Where it likely fails: selection by the vote is the likely failure; its plausible direction is attenuation. The mismatched group is itself selected on voting against its attachment, and mixes strategic
  voters, multiple party ID, recall error and matching artefacts
  ────────────────────────────────────────
  Outcome family: Horizontal behavioral AP
  What the contrast buys: the partner's party is randomized, so $AP_t$ is a causal effect of the partner label for each type; the control splits favoritism from derogation; same respondents as the thermometer
  give a within-person attitudinal vs. behavioral comparison
  Boundaries: $\Delta AP$ is how a causal effect varies by a non-randomized moderator, so it is descriptive; few co-partisan partners for deniers and few vote-only partners for mismatched respondents; the
  party
  label also carries inferred policy; one election year
  Causal reading also needs: the same ignorability of type as above
  Where it likely fails: ΔAP inherits every confounding problem of type; only the effect of the partner label is experimental

  Table 3: building the model step by step

  The same estimand (g-computed marginal-mean contrasts with stated weights) is computed at every step, so the steps can be compared directly.

  ┌──────┬─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┬─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┬──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ Step │                           Layer added                           │                           What it contributes                           │                   What to compare                    │
  ├──────┼─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┼─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┼──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │ 1    │ Likelihood on one survey                                        │ a family that reproduces the outcome's shape and cell means             │ posterior predictive checks by cell                  │
  ├──────┼─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┼─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┼──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │ 2    │ Party within country (plus respondent and target layers for     │ the within-party contrast, assuming one common gap. The benchmark       │ against raw within-party cell means                  │
  │      │ repeated outcomes)                                              │                                                                         │                                                      │
  ├──────┼─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┼─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┼──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │ 3    │ Contrast varying by country                                     │ comparative inference with partial pooling: the comparative figure      │ how much countries differ, relative to the prior     │
  ├──────┼─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┼─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┼──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │ 4    │ Contrast varying by party                                       │ heterogeneity across parties; the estimand uses your stated weights     │ a shift from step 2 means the gap varies with party  │
  │      │                                                                 │ rather than implicit precision weights                                  │ composition                                          │
  ├──────┼─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┼─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┼──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │ 5    │ Dual party membership for mismatched respondents (attachment    │ separates attachment from vote in one model                             │ against fits that code only one in-party             │
  │      │ party and vote party)                                           │                                                                         │                                                      │
  ├──────┼─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┼─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┼──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │ 6    │ Study and wording layer (pooling across sources)                │ one European scale across operationalizations                           │ separate per-study fits as triangulation             │
  ├──────┼─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┼─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┼──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │ 7    │ Time: surveys within countries, type-specific smooth trends     │ dynamic inference: the over-time figure, and the decomposition          │ stability when single studies are dropped; trends    │
  │      │ varying by country                                              │                                                                         │ vs. switching between studies                        │
  ├──────┼─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┼─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┼──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │ 8    │ Distributional layer (dispersion by cell)                       │ calibrated uncertainty by cell                                          │ predictive checks and calibration by cell            │
  ├──────┼─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┼─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┼──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │ 9    │ Diagnostics and adjustments: policy distance, benchmark, party  │ the party-vs.-policy tests; identification robustness                   │ adjusted vs. unadjusted; sensitivity to an           │
  │      │ position, pre-treatment covariates                              │                                                                         │ unobserved confounder                                │
  └──────┴─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┴─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┴──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  Alongside every step:
  - Prior sensitivity: the variance components of small groups lean on the prior.
  - Uncorrelated varying effects as a check.
  - Fake-data simulation from step 4 on, recovering known contrasts at your real cell sizes.

  For the games: steps 1–5, 8 and 9 apply; there is no study or time layer.

  Bringing the outcomes together

  - Party-over-policy profile: the pattern of type contrasts across the six polarization outcomes, set against the predictions of each account. Write it down before fitting.
  - Sorting adds the opinion-structure prediction. If partisanship bundles positions, attached partisans should be more aligned, and see the party system as more aligned, than deniers.
  - Decomposition over time and across countries for outcomes 1–5: change in the type mix vs. change within types.
  - Attitudinal vs. behavioral only within eu25 (same respondents, standardized). The EES 2024 horizontal-attitudinal panel separates target from measurement mode, but descriptively, since it uses different
    respondents and a different year.
